newsitem.title: USA: US House tax panel defeats child credit proposals.
newsitem.headline: US House tax panel defeats child credit proposals.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee finished consideration of a child tax credit portion of a wide-ranging tax bill early Thursday, defeating proposals from Democrats who said the Republican plan did not help lower-income families.

The House Ways and Means Committee started work on a proposal from Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, of how to accomplish the $85 billion in tax cuts agreed to in a budget pact between congressional Republicans and the White House.

The child tax credit is the single biggest item in the proposed tax bill at a cost of $71 billion over five years. Under Archer's plan, families would receive a $400 tax credit in 1998 for each child under age 17, increased to $500 in following years.
Democrats and the White House have attacked Archer's tax bill, saying it favoured wealthier Americans over the poor. Archer says the plan gives the most benefit to the middle class.
"Clearly this is not everything the president would want, we have made significant progress. It's not everything I want," Archer said at the start of the meeting.

The committee spent four hours deliberating provisions in the whole bill and then spent three more hours considering amendments to the first of 16 sections. The committee was scheduled to resume work on the bill starting at 10:00 a.m. EDT Thursday.
Democrats offered amendments to restructure the proposed child tax credit, offsetting any increased costs by scaling back on proposed capital gains tax reductions.
Capital gains tax relief is one of the main items that Republicans want to achieve in the tax cut legislation.

The amendments were defeated along party-line votes. Archer at one point reminded sponsors of the amendments that a capital gains tax cut was important to Republicans and that proposals to the contrary would result in a "small tug-of-war."
All tax legislation must originate in the House Ways and Means committee.
Archer's legislation also includes tax incentives for higher education and a reduction in the capital gains tax.
Archer made some last-minute changes to his initial proposals on inheritance tax relief and extending the airline ticket tax.

The estate tax change would gradually increase the threshold where estate taxes kick in to $1 million in 2007 from the current $600,000. Previously in Archer's bill that $1 million mark would have been reached in 2014.
That change would more than double the cost of the estate tax relief to $7.5 billion over five years from the previous $3.1 billion.
The increase would be paid for by reducing the cost of the corporate alternative minimum tax proposal. Under the change, that tax would be repealed only for small businesses, not large corporations.

Another change in Archer's bill would earmark funds from a 4.3 cents-per-gallon tax on aviation gasoline and jet fuel for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund that pays for airport repairs and improvements. Initially the money from that tax would have been put in the general fund.
The revised Archer bill would also not apply domestic air transportation taxes to the domestic leg of an international flight as previously proposed.

Representative Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, offered an amendment to increase the cigarette tax to 53 cents a pack from 24 cents to fund children's health insurance, but withdrew it because children's health insurance is not under the committee's jurisdiction.
She planned to introduce the cigarette tax increase proposal again, without tying it to children's health insurance.
